meta.title: More you can do: messaging, scopes, rules, expiring notes
meta.description: Beyond handoffs: send a request from one project’s agent to another’s inbox, keep clients and mono-repos apart, pin rules, write notes that expire.

hero.title: More you can do
hero.lede: Handoffs and search are the daily use. These are the other things a memory that lives in one server can do for you, from passing work between projects to keeping a client’s memory apart from another’s.

messaging.title: One agent asks another project’s agent for something
messaging.lede: Two repositories that talk over an API, each with its own agent and its own memory. The frontend agent knows the protocol. Instead of reading the whole API repository, it writes a complete request and drops it in that project’s inbox.
messaging.figureAlt: Diagram: an agent in project A sends a sealed request through the memory server into project B’s inbox, where an agent claims it once and reads an API specification. A wall between the projects marks that no context is shared, and the received message is treated as untrusted input.
messaging.figureCaption: Only the envelope crosses. Project A never reads project B’s files, and project B never reads project A’s.

example.title: What it looks like
example.send: > Ask the agent in default/api to add a /v1/export endpoint that streams NDJSON, keep the existing auth middleware, and send it through ai-memory.
example.sendResult: The agent calls memory_message_send with a self-contained body. The request has to stand on its own, because the reader cannot see this project.
example.notice: 📬 ai-memory: 1 cross-project message waiting in this project’s inbox.
example.receiveResult: The agent calls memory_message_pop, gets the request with who sent it, and works from it. A second pop returns nothing.

points.title: Addressed to a project
points.text: A message goes to a workspace and project, and any session in that project can claim it. Once claimed, it is gone from the queue, like a handoff.

points.title: Nothing enters context by itself
points.text: The session start notice carries only a count. Message text reaches an agent through a deliberate pop, fenced and marked as untrusted, with the sender shown outside the fence.

points.title: Fails closed
points.text: The recipient project must exist, so a typo is rejected instead of landing in an inbox nobody reads. Each inbox holds at most 256 pending messages.

points.title: Retractable, audited
points.text: The sender can cancel a message until it is claimed. Secrets are scrubbed on send, the body is size-capped, and on a shared server every message records who sent it.

cli.c2: In the other project: list without consuming, or claim the oldest
cli.c3: Change your mind before it is claimed

scopes.title: Keep clients, mono-repos and personal work apart
scopes.lede: Memory is filed by workspace and project. A checkout with a git remote is filed by that remote, so the same repository cloned twice shares one memory, and a folder without a remote uses its name. A small file changes the rest.
scopes.figureAlt: Diagram: three folders, each with a .ai-memory.toml marker, map to separate workspaces inside one memory server. One workspace holds a mono-repo whose directories share a project. To the side sit a pinned rules page, a note that expires on Friday, and a page with feedback.
scopes.figureCaption: One server, separate shelves. The marker file decides which shelf a directory lands on.

items.title: One workspace per client
items.text: Drop .ai-memory.toml in ~/work/client-a/ and every repository below it files under that workspace. Nothing from client A ever surfaces while you work for client B.

items.title: A mono-repo as one project
items.text: A marker that names a project pins every subdirectory to it, so packages share one memory. Leave the project out and each package keeps its own.

items.title: Git worktrees
items.text: Linked worktrees resolve to the main repository, so a branch checked out elsewhere keeps the same memory.

items.title: Two agents in one project
items.text: The current-project pointer is isolated per caller, so Claude Code and Codex can run side by side in the same directory without confusing each other.

items.title: One laptop, two employers
items.text: Register each server with ai-memory server add and name it in the marker with server = "team-b". Hooks from that tree go there and nowhere else, and a name that does not resolve sends nothing.

items.title: Pin an identity
items.text: identity = "acme/platform" files a checkout under that key wherever it lives, even with no remote.

scopes.codeComment: Every repository under this directory files under the client-a workspace

rules.title: Rules that reach every session
rules.lede: Tell the agent to remember something permanently and it becomes a page in the wiki. Rules are filed apart from facts, and the session brief can put them in front of the agent before the first prompt.

items.title: Say it once
items.text: “Remember: before touching the payment code, read the PCI notes.” The agent writes a durable page. Ask for it as a global rule and it applies to all your projects.

items.title: The brief carries them in
items.text: With inject_on_session_start = true in the project’s marker file, pinned pages, rules and slots are prepended to every new session’s context.

items.title: Lint suggests promotion
items.text: When a rule looks durable enough, memory_lint suggests copying it into CLAUDE.md or AGENTS.md. ai-memory never edits those files itself.

items.title: Decision records stay yours
items.text: ai-memory never writes into your repository. Keep an ADR directory, and list it under [capture] ignore_paths so the wiki does not keep a stale copy of it.

rules.codeComment: Prepend pinned pages, rules and slots to every session

notes.title: Notes that expire, and feedback that reorders

items.title: Remember this until Friday
items.text: A page written with expires_at drops out of search after that date. It is still there for a search that asks for expired pages.

items.title: That page was wrong
items.text: memory_feedback records helpful, not helpful, stale or wrong on a page. Stale and wrong lower it in future rankings and speed up its aging. Feedback never deletes.

items.title: Move a session
items.text: A session captured in the wrong project, after a cd into a scratch directory, can be reattached with ai-memory move-session. Its observations and page move with it.

items.title: Recover from compaction
items.text: When Claude Code or Codex compact their context, a hook writes a fresh session page first, so what was compacted away can be recalled.

browse.title: Read it in a browser, take it anywhere

items.title: A read-only web UI
items.text: Start the server with --enable-web and every project’s pages are browsable, grouped into concepts, decisions, gotchas and sessions, with a JSON API under /api/v1.

items.title: An open format
items.text: Each project is an Open Knowledge Format bundle. ai-memory export-okf packages it for any tool that reads OKF, and the files are plain markdown for everything else.

items.title: Skills for your agent
items.text: ai-memory install-mcp also installs a short routing snippet and managed Agent Skills, so the agent knows which tool answers “have we discussed this?” and which sends mail.

operate.title: Chores the launcher takes on
operate.lede: ai-memory run starts the agent through the memory server. It also keeps the binary current, closes sessions and says so before it disarms anything.
operate.figureAlt: Diagram: a terminal running ai-memory run in the center. Around it: a sandbox that the launcher offers before disarming safety prompts, a download with a checksum for the self-upgrade, a session page that closes when the agent exits, and a browser sign-in for the web UI.
operate.figureCaption: One command in the middle. The rest happens around it without a second tool.

items.title: Upgrade in one command
items.text: ai-memory upgrade downloads the matching release, checks the checksum, swaps the binary and refreshes the hooks. Docker, Homebrew, AUR and RPM installs keep their own path.

items.title: A warning before the guard rails come off
items.text: ai-memory run --yolo says what it is about to disarm and, on Linux and macOS with ai-jail usable, offers to re-run the session inside the sandbox with a checklist of what the jail may see. --jail goes straight in with sensible defaults.

items.title: Environment for the harness
items.text: --env KEY=VALUE and --env-file reach the spawned agent and ai-memory’s own session lookup, so a per-account CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR needs no wrapper script.

items.title: Sessions close on exit
items.text: Agents with no session-end hook (Command Code, Kiro CLI, Antigravity CLI) get their summary and handoff when the launcher exits. finalize-session --reopen covers a conversation that went on afterwards.

items.title: Sign in to the web UI
items.text: The built-in wiki has login and change-password pages for password users, and a root-only page to approve or reject pending auto-improvement proposals across projects.

items.title: Stopwords in your language
items.text: [search.fts] stopwords lists the function words of your language, so full-text ranking on a Portuguese wiki is not skewed by de and que.

faq.q: Can an agent in one project read another project’s memory?
faq.a: No. Memory is filed per project, and messaging is the one deliberate crossing: a project sees only mail addressed to it or sent by it. The message body has to be self-contained because the reader cannot see the sender’s files.

faq.q: Is a received message treated as instructions?
faq.a: No. A popped message is fenced as untrusted cross-project input and carries a notice saying so. The agent evaluates it as a task request with you, and the sender is shown outside the fence so you can judge trust first.

faq.q: What happens if two sessions check the same inbox?
faq.a: The first pop claims the message and the second gets nothing. A message is claimed exactly once, the same rule handoffs follow.

faq.q: Do I have to configure workspaces?
faq.a: No. Without a marker file, everything files under a workspace called default, with the git remote as the project, or the directory name when there is none. Add .ai-memory.toml only when you want client separation, a mono-repo as one project, work and personal memory kept apart, or a second server.
